analysis.one_liner: Hands federal coal strip-mine enforcement to the states and limits citizen lawsuits over mine violations.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: after one subcommittee hearing in May 1996, the Senate never acted on it before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the 1977 law governing strip coal mining so that states with approved programs — not the federal Office of Surface Mining — would be the only permitter and enforcer of mining and reclamation rules. It would deem any operation following its state permit automatically compliant with federal standards, cut citizen lawsuits and federal inspections, bar enforcement actions started more than three years after a violation, and take public roads out of the regulated definition of a mining operation. It never got past a Senate subcommittee hearing.
analysis.who_benefits: Coal mining companies. They would gain a single state regulator instead of overlapping federal and state oversight, a guarantee that following their permit satisfies all environmental standards, a three-year limit on enforcement of old violations, exemption for public haul roads, and state-court review that is harder for citizens to use. States with approved programs would also gain exclusive control over mining within their borders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coal mining companies and state regulators

how_it_helps.text: States with approved programs would have 'sole responsibility' for issuing violation notices and suspending or revoking permits, subject only to state review — ending the federal Office of Surface Mining's independent inspections and enforcement orders in those states.

Any operation in compliance with its permit would be 'deemed to be in compliance' with all federal and state environmental protection standards, so regulators could not apply new or stricter requirements without formally revising the permit.
A new three-year statute of limitations would bar any enforcement action, fine, or penalty unless started within three years of the violation first occurring.

The definition of a regulated surface coal mining operation would no longer cover the construction, improvement, or use of public roads, removing haul-road construction from federal reclamation and water-protection rules.

Judicial review would be reshaped in operators' favor: challenges to state regulatory decisions would go only to state courts, a citizen-suit preservation provision would be repealed, and federal enforcement actions would be reviewed by the U.S. district court containing the state's capital.

analysis.who_pays: People who live near coal mines, and taxpayers. Without federal inspections and citizen suits, water pollution, blasting damage, and unreclaimed mined land would depend entirely on each state's willingness and budget to enforce; a three-year time limit would let older violations escape penalties; and cleanup costs that companies avoid could fall on the abandoned-mine reclamation fund and local communities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Mine neighbors, water users, and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the federal backstop: the Office of Surface Mining could no longer independently inspect, issue cessation orders, or override lax state enforcement in states with approved programs, and the provision preserving citizens' rights to sue in federal court would be repealed.

The three-year statute of limitations would bar enforcement of violations — including long-running water pollution or reclamation failures — discovered or acted on more than three years after they began.
The 'deemed compliance' rule would lock in the standards written into each permit, so an operation could keep mining under outdated conditions even after federal or state rules were strengthened.

Supporters would argue this is genuine federalism: most coal states already run approved programs, and eliminating duplicate federal inspections saves money without weakening reclamation on the ground.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the coal industry the savings are real but administrative: less paperwork, one regulator, fewer surprise federal orders, and a hard deadline on old violations. The costs are shifted onto the public — weaker water-quality enforcement near mines, fewer avenues for citizens to challenge violations, and possible taxpayer liability for land and water damage the operators no longer fear being made to fix. The bill offers no offsetting protection for the communities that absorb strip mining's effects, so on balance its benefits are concentrated and its costs diffuse.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and its forests subcommittee, got a single hearing in May 1996, and never received a markup or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Bennett introduced the bill on November 8, 1995, joined by Senators Thomas, Simpson, Warner, and Hatch, with seven Republican cosponsors in all.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, which sent it to the Subcommittee on Forests and Public Lands the next day.
The subcommittee held the bill's only hearing on May 2, 1996 (printed as S.Hrg. 104-528); no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed.
The bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, with the bill still stuck in subcommittee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the federal Office of Surface Mining kept its inspection and enforcement authority and citizens kept federal-court remedies, so communities near coal mines are no worse off than before. Coal companies and state regulators, who stood to gain sole control and shorter enforcement deadlines, got nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Every Senate backer on the record — the sponsor and all seven cosponsors — was a Republican, and no Democrat signed on; no vote was ever taken to test broader support.

industries.note: The bill would end duplicate federal inspections, guarantee that permit compliance satisfies all standards, impose a three-year deadline on enforcement, and exempt public haul roads — cutting compliance costs and legal exposure. Those savings come at the expense of water quality, reclamation, and citizen oversight for the people living around the mines.

States with approved programs would become the sole permitter and enforcer, with federal rules inapplicable until the state itself amends its program. State agencies gain authority and discretion, though they would bear full enforcement responsibility without a federal backstop.

The bill repeals the citizen-suit preservation provision and channels challenges into state courts, removing the main tools citizen groups use to force action against mine operators. Their loss tracks directly with the public's loss of an enforcement backstop.

industries.industry: Federal Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement
industries.note: The bill strikes the office's oversight functions and makes its rules inapplicable in states with approved programs, reducing it to a program approver rather than an active regulator. Its enforcement role is the main protection ordinary people would lose if the bill became law.
